"We truly hope that they are remembered for the way they lived their lives and not this tragic end," Charlstie Laytin said in a telephone interview Wednesday. "We're all just devastated and going to miss them both so much." The Harrises were two of three Americans on board Air France Flight 447 when it crashed Monday. The plane was carrying 228 passengers and crew from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, France, when it crashed four hours into the journey. Investigators have not determined the cause of the accident. An official list with the victims' names was not available Wednesday afternoon. The Harrises lived in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Anne Harris' sister, Mary Miley, said. Michael Harris, 60, was a geologist in Rio de Janeiro. He worked for Devon Energy, a U.S.-based independent natural gas and oil producer, a company spokesman said. The couple were traveling to Paris for a training seminar and vacation, Miley said. The two "loved everyone, they loved life," Laytin said. "Definitely glass-half-full kind of people," she added, recalling her uncle as a "ham," who could always offer a laugh on a bad day. She remembered a moment a few summers ago when her family was in Vermont, and had just seen a classical performance of Mozart. They were "just sitting around and having a glass of wine, and laughing and talking about family and life and what was going on in our lives ... [the Harrises] could never get enough information about what all their nieces and nephews and family members were doing," she said. "It's really the last time I can remember us all sitting around as a family and I'm so glad that I have that memory." She said her family was hopeful the investigation would soon determine what had gone wrong. "I think the initial shock of it all has really started to wear off, and the reality that they're gone is starting to set in," she said. "The grief and the grieving process is beginning and we're just really focused on helping each other heal." The majority of the people on the flight came from Brazil, France and Germany. The remaining victims were from 29 other countries. Ten were employees of French electrical equipment supplier CGED, according to Agence France-Presse. Nine of those employees had won the trip to Rio from CGED because of their strong work performance, AFP said. "There was a competition for the best sales reps ... and nine of them won and went to Brazil for four days," Laurent Bouveresse, CGED chief executive, told AFP. The nine were allowed to take a friend or partner, and an executive also went along, Bouveresse said, according to the news agency. CNN tried repeatedly to reach representatives of CGED. Two others believed to have been on the flight were an engaged couple, Julia Schmidt of Brazil and Alex Crolow of Germany, the couple's friend, Brian Buzby of Houston, Texas, told CNN affiliate KTRK.  Watch Buzby talk about friends on Flight 447 » . Buzby said he met the two while they were all students at Bucerius Law School in Germany. They finished studies last August, KTRK reported. "This was Alex taking her back to tell her mom they were going to get married," Buzby told KTRK. "I just hope that they were not suffering, and at least they were together, because I would have hated for one of them to go through it alone," Buzby said. "They were my two best friends. I just hope she knows I loved her," Buzby said.

Charlstie Laytin, the niece of Anne and Michael Harris, said the pair “loved life” and “loved everyone.”

“Our sincere hope is that people remember them for how they lived, rather than for this heartbreaking ending,” Laytin said Wednesday during a phone interview. “All of us are devastated, and we are going to miss them both terribly.”

The Harrises were among three Americans aboard Air France Flight 447, which went down Monday. The aircraft had 228 passengers and crew members on board and was traveling from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, France, when it crashed about four hours after takeoff. Authorities had not yet identified the cause of the crash. As of Wednesday afternoon, an official passenger list naming the victims had not been released.

Anne Harris’ sister, Mary Miley, said the couple lived in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Michael Harris, 60, worked there as a geologist for Devon Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company based in the United States, a company spokesperson said.

Miley said the couple had been heading to Paris for both a training seminar and a vacation.

Laytin described them as people who “loved everyone” and “loved life,” adding that they were “definitely glass-half-full kind of people.” She remembered her uncle as a natural entertainer, someone who could make others laugh even on a difficult day.

She recalled one summer several years earlier, when her family was in Vermont after attending a classical Mozart performance. They were “sitting around and having a glass of wine, and laughing and talking about family and life and what was going on in our lives,” she said. The Harrises, she added, were always eager to hear every detail about what their nieces, nephews and other relatives were doing.

“It’s really the last time I can remember us all sitting around as a family, and I’m so glad that I have that memory,” Laytin said.

She said relatives were hoping investigators would soon learn what caused the disaster.

“I think the first shock of it has really begun to fade, and the reality that they are gone is beginning to sink in,” she said. “The grief and the grieving process are starting, and right now we’re focused on helping one another heal.”

Most of the passengers and crew members aboard the flight were from Brazil, France and Germany. The other victims came from 29 additional countries.

Ten of those on board were employees of CGED, a French supplier of electrical equipment, according to Agence France-Presse. AFP reported that nine of the employees had earned the trip to Rio de Janeiro from CGED because of their strong job performance.

“There was a competition for the best sales reps ... and nine of them won and went to Brazil for four days,” Laurent Bouveresse, CGED’s chief executive, told AFP.

Bouveresse said the nine winners were permitted to bring a friend or partner, and that a company executive also joined the trip, according to the news agency.

CNN made repeated attempts to contact CGED representatives.

Two others believed to have been aboard were an engaged couple: Julia Schmidt of Brazil and Alex Crolow of Germany, their friend Brian Buzby of Houston, Texas, told CNN affiliate KTRK.

Buzby said he had met them when all three were students at Bucerius Law School in Germany. KTRK reported that they completed their studies the previous August.

“This was Alex taking her back to tell her mom they were going to get married,” Buzby told KTRK.

“I just hope that they were not suffering, and at least they were together, because I would have hated for one of them to go through it alone,” Buzby said.

“They were my two best friends. I just hope she knows I loved her,” he added.

**Lives Carried Across the Atlantic: Remembering the Passengers of Air France Flight 447**

When Air France Flight 447 lifted off from Rio de Janeiro on the night of May 31, 2009, it carried more than travelers bound for Paris. It carried families returning home, businesspeople between continents, newlyweds, children, students, engineers, doctors, artists, and loved ones who had promised to call after landing.

The Airbus A330 disappeared over the Atlantic in the early hours of June 1. All 228 people aboard — 216 passengers and 12 crew members — were lost. In the years since, the disaster has often been discussed through the language of aviation: weather systems, pitot tubes, cockpit alarms, deep-sea searches, flight data recorders. But behind the technical record remains the deeper human one: a manifest of individual lives, each leaving behind a circle of grief.

Among those remembered were Anne and Michael Harris, a couple whose names became part of the long list of victims mourned across nations. To their family and friends, they were not statistics in one of aviation’s most studied tragedies, but familiar voices, habits, stories, and affections — the intimate details by which the dead remain present among the living.

Relatives of those aboard Flight 447 have often spoken of the strange cruelty of such a loss: the sudden break in ordinary life, the distance of the ocean, and the absence of a final goodbye. For the Harris family, as for so many others, remembrance came not only through public memorials but through private rituals — photographs kept close, conversations repeated, birthdays marked, and memories shared so that Anne and Michael would not be defined by the manner of their deaths.

They were remembered as part of a family story that continued after them, a story shaped by love, disbelief, and endurance. In the aftermath of the crash, families of victims were bound together by a grief that crossed language and nationality. Many had never met before, yet they found themselves linked by the same unanswered questions and the same need to recover not only the aircraft, but the truth of what had happened to the people they loved.

Flight 447 was strikingly international. Its passengers came from dozens of countries, reflecting the global nature of the route between Brazil and France. Brazilians made up the largest group aboard, followed by French citizens, but the manifest also included people from Germany, Italy, China, the United Kingdom, Spain, Switzerland, Ireland, Argentina, the United States, and other nations. Some were returning from holidays in Brazil; others were traveling for work, study, or family obligations. Several were couples. Some were parents traveling with children. Others were young professionals whose lives seemed to be opening before them.

That international makeup shaped the mourning that followed. Vigils were held on both sides of the Atlantic. In Brazil, families gathered near the coast, looking out toward the ocean that had swallowed the plane. In France, services and memorials drew relatives into a shared public sorrow. Embassies, churches, airports, and private homes became places of waiting and remembrance.

For weeks, then months, then years, the Atlantic remained central to the story. Search teams faced immense depths and difficult terrain before the wreckage and flight recorders were finally recovered from the ocean floor in 2011. For investigators, the discovery brought crucial evidence. For families, it brought something more complicated: a measure of certainty, but not relief; answers, but not restoration.

The legacy of Flight 447 is now inseparable from reforms in aviation training and safety, but for the families it is also preserved in quieter ways. It lives in names read aloud at memorial ceremonies. It lives in children growing up with stories of relatives they lost or never had the chance to know. It lives in the determination of families to insist that each passenger be remembered as a person, not merely as part of a total.

Anne and Michael Harris were two among 228, yet like every person aboard, they represented an entire world to those who loved them. Their absence became part of their family’s history, carried forward in memory rather than presence.

The story of Air France Flight 447 is therefore not only the story of a crash. It is the story of lives interrupted between continents, of families joined by grief, and of an international community of mourners who learned that the measure of such a tragedy is not only in the number lost, but in the countless bonds broken when a plane never arrives.

(CNN) -- Anne and Michael Harris were an “extraordinary” couple, the kind of people friends say made others feel instantly welcome, whether at a dinner table, on a long walk or in a brief conversation that somehow lingered for years.

Now their family, like the relatives of more than 200 others aboard Air France Flight 447, is struggling to reconcile those vivid memories with the vast emptiness of the Atlantic Ocean, where the Paris-bound jet disappeared after leaving Rio de Janeiro.

The Airbus A330 was carrying 228 people when it went down early Monday on a flight from Brazil to France. Passengers included business travelers, vacationers, students, parents and children — lives that had briefly converged inside one aircraft and are now being mourned across continents.

In the days since the crash, relatives have gathered at airports, churches and crisis centers, waiting for information while officials coordinate an immense search effort across a remote stretch of ocean. For many families, the absence of answers has deepened the grief.

“We keep expecting the phone to ring,” one relative said. “You know it won’t, but you still listen for it.”

Friends of the Harrises described them as devoted to each other and deeply engaged in the lives of those around them. They were remembered as generous hosts, enthusiastic travelers and people whose warmth seemed effortless.

“They were extraordinary because they made ordinary moments feel special,” a family friend said. “That is what everyone is holding on to now.”

The crash has left communities around the world mourning. In France and Brazil, officials have offered condolences and promised a thorough investigation. Search crews have scoured thousands of square miles of ocean for wreckage, while aviation experts say recovering flight data recorders from deep water could be crucial to understanding what happened.

But for grieving families, the technical questions are only one part of the tragedy. They are also beginning the painful work of telling stories — of careers cut short, children left without parents, parents left without children, and couples whose futures ended together.

At memorial gatherings, photographs have been placed beside candles and flowers. Some relatives have spoken publicly; others have asked for privacy. Many have described the same feeling: a sudden, almost incomprehensible rupture.

Air France has said it is assisting families and cooperating with investigators. French and Brazilian authorities have said the search and recovery effort will continue, though difficult weather, deep water and the remote location have complicated operations.

For those who loved the Harrises, and for families of all aboard Flight 447, remembrance has become a way to resist the anonymity of disaster.

“They were not just names on a passenger list,” one mourner said. “They were loved. They were cherished. And they will be missed every day.”
